activate-public-space-bring-a-neighborho.title: Activate Public Space: Bring a Neighborhood Dog Park to Eagle Hill
activate-public-space-bring-a-neighborho.description_full:
We respectfully call upon the Boston Planning Department, Boston Parks & Recreation Department, our District 1 City Councilor, and all relevant City agencies to evaluate and authorize the interim activation of a portion of the existing paved area at 146 Condor Street, East Boston, as a public Dog Recreation Space (DRS) while also evaluating opportunities for its long-term preservation as a permanent neighborhood recreational amenity.

This proposal presents a practical, low-impact opportunity to activate an existing paved area for immediate public benefit while remaining compatible with future waterfront planning, environmental requirements, and potential maritime redevelopment.

The proposed location was selected because it utilizes an existing paved surface, minimizes site disturbance, and can be implemented with relatively modest infrastructure improvements while preserving flexibility for future planning.

 


Why This Matters

Eagle Hill is one of Boston’s most densely populated neighborhoods, yet it lacks a dedicated fenced off-leash Dog Recreation Space. Many Eagle Hill residents own dogs, but there is no safe location within walking distance where they can legally exercise, socialize, and play.

Without a designated space, many residents are forced to use sidewalks, parking lots, or other public areas not intended for off-leash recreation. A neighborhood Dog Recreation Space would improve public safety, encourage responsible pet ownership, promote physical activity, and provide a welcoming gathering place that strengthens community connections.

Meanwhile, an existing paved portion of 146 Condor Street is not currently used for public recreation. We respectfully request that only a small portion to be activated to meet this immediate neighborhood need while preserving flexibility for future planning and redevelopment.

 


Our Proposal

We propose creating a professionally designed Dog Recreation Space featuring:

Separate fenced areas for large and small dogs
Double-gated safety entrances
ADA-accessible pathways
Agility and enrichment equipment
Dog drinking fountains
Waste bag dispensers and disposal stations
Benches and shaded seating
Landscaping and privacy screening where appropriate
Durable, low-maintenance surface materials suitable for year-round use
The Dog Recreation Space would complement the surrounding neighborhood while requiring only minimal modifications to the existing paved site.

 


Phase 1 – Interim Community Activation

We respectfully request that the City evaluate the feasibility of activating the existing paved footprint using a low-impact design that minimizes site disturbance.

The proposal prioritizes use of the existing pavement and improvements that minimize—or eliminate—excavation whenever practicable. Utilizing the existing paved surface reduces construction impacts while maintaining flexibility for future site planning and environmental compliance.

This approach provides immediate public benefits while allowing the City to continue evaluating long-term planning opportunities for the property.

 


Phase 2 – Long-Term Evaluation

Following successful interim activation, we respectfully request that the City evaluate opportunities to incorporate this recreational footprint into future Chelsea River waterfront planning and broader neighborhood open-space initiatives.

This proposal is designed to complement—not replace—the City’s long-term vision for the property by demonstrating how a small portion of the site can provide immediate public benefit while preserving future maritime, industrial, and waterfront redevelopment opportunities.

Whenever feasible, the long-term goal is to preserve this community amenity as part of East Boston’s growing network of public recreational spaces.

 


Community Benefits

This project would:

Create a new recreational space.
Provide a safe, enclosed area for off-leash dog exercise.
Encourage responsible pet ownership.
Promote physical activity and outdoor recreation.
Strengthen neighborhood connections.
Improve cleanliness through dedicated pet waste stations.
Activate an existing paved area with minimal construction.
Increase access to neighborhood open space.
Improve quality of life for residents and visitors.

 

Community Stewardship

This initiative is community-driven.

In partnership with the City, neighborhood volunteers intend to establish the Friends of the Eagle Hill Dog Recreation Space, a volunteer stewardship organization dedicated to supporting the facility through:

Volunteer cleanup days
Community fundraising
Beautification projects
Educational outreach
Park advocacy
Promoting responsible use
The Friends group would serve as a volunteer partner to Boston Parks & Recreation, complementing—not replacing—City maintenance responsibilities while demonstrating the neighborhood’s long-term commitment to keeping the space clean, safe, and welcoming.

 


Community Support

This proposal reflects growing grassroots support from Eagle Hill residents, dog owners, nearby neighbors, and other community stakeholders who recognize the need for additional neighborhood open space and safe off-leash recreation.

Hundreds of residents have already signed the petition in support of creating a neighborhood Dog Recreation Space, and community support continues to grow. Community members continue engaging neighbors and gathering signatures to demonstrate broad public interest in creating this much-needed public amenity.

 


Working with the City

Should the City determine that this proposal is feasible, community volunteers are prepared to work collaboratively with Boston Parks & Recreation throughout the Dog Recreation Space application, public engagement, design, permitting, and implementation process established under City regulations.

We welcome the opportunity to partner with City staff, neighborhood organizations, environmental stakeholders, nearby businesses, and elected officials to ensure the project is thoughtfully planned, responsibly managed, and serves the best interests of the community.

 


Why Now?

Boston has an opportunity to demonstrate how thoughtful, low-impact activation of an existing paved public space can deliver meaningful community benefits while preserving flexibility for future redevelopment.

By utilizing only. the existing paved frontage, this proposal represents a practical investment in recreation, public health, neighborhood connectivity, public safety, and quality of life without limiting future planning opportunities. It is an achievable, community-focused project capable of delivering lasting public benefits with relatively modest infrastructure improvements.

 


Take Action

If you believe Eagle Hill deserves a safe, dedicated place where dogs can exercise responsibly and neighbors can gather, connect, and build community, please add your name in support of this initiative.

Together, we can demonstrate that thoughtful planning, community collaboration, and responsible stewardship can transform a small portion of existing public space into a lasting neighborhood asset for Eagle Hill.

Please sign the petition and help bring the Eagle Hill Dog Recreation Space to life.

implement-resident-only-overnight-parkin.title: Implement resident-only overnight parking in Jeffries Point
implement-resident-only-overnight-parkin.description_full:
Living in Jeffries Point, East Boston, has been a cherished experience for many of us. We appreciate the vibrant community and the active lifestyle it promotes. However, like many urban neighborhoods, parking has become a growing concern. Residents here face difficulty in finding parking near their homes, particularly during evening and overnight hours when many non-residents park in the area. This causes distress and inconvenience that impacts our daily lives.

In order to address this, we are urging Mayor Michelle Wu and the City of Boston to implement resident-only parking from 6:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m., during the week and weekends open parking for visitors as well but no commerical parking overnight at all across our beloved Jeffries Point. This change not only ensures that residents can find parking near their homes but also helps to manage overflows of non-resident vehicles that continuously exploit the current system at our expense.

Parking scarcity can lead to a range of problems—heightened stress for families returning home after a long day, concerns over the safety of walking long distances late at night, and complications for our senior residents and families with young children. Our proposal is not merely about convenience; it is a plea for enhancing the quality of life, safety, and community continuity.

The positive impact of this proposal can be supported by examples from similar initiatives in neighborhoods like South Boston, where resident-only parking has led to improved conditions and greater community satisfaction. These policies have helped maintain neighborhood integrity and reduced unnecessary traffic, which benefits all.

Our community has shown resilience and adaptability in the face of many challenges, but parking is a persistent issue that requires thoughtful policy interventions. By considering the request for designated resident-only parking hours, the City of Boston can demonstrate its commitment to community welfare and urban livability.

We believe that with balanced policy adjustments, such as properly managed signage and strict enforcement during resident-only hours, this initiative can be successfully implemented without significant disruption to other city services or neighboring areas.

Your support is crucial in making Jeffries Point a more livable place for its families and long-time residents. Please join us in signing this petition to make a significant positive change for our neighborhood.

 

 

El Problema
Vivir en Jeffries Point, East Boston, ha sido una experiencia muy apreciada por muchos de nosotros. Valoramos nuestra comunidad vibrante y el estilo de vida activo que promueve. Sin embargo, como ocurre en muchos vecindarios urbanos, el estacionamiento se ha convertido en una preocupación cada vez mayor. Los residentes enfrentamos dificultades para encontrar estacionamiento cerca de nuestros hogares, particularmente durante las horas de la tarde y la noche, cuando muchas personas que no viven en el vecindario estacionan sus vehículos en la zona. Esto genera estrés, preocupación e inconvenientes que afectan nuestra vida cotidiana.

Para abordar esta situación, estamos solicitando al Alcalde Michelle Wu y a la Ciudad de Boston que implementen estacionamiento exclusivo para residentes de 6:00 p.m. a 8:00 a.m., de lunes a domingo, permitiendo durante el día el estacionamiento abierto para visitantes. Asimismo, solicitamos que no se permita el estacionamiento comercial durante la noche en todo nuestro querido Jeffries Point.

Este cambio no solo garantizaría que los residentes puedan encontrar estacionamiento cerca de sus hogares, sino que también ayudaría a controlar la gran cantidad de vehículos de personas que no viven en el vecindario y que constantemente aprovechan el sistema actual a costa de los residentes.

La escasez de estacionamiento puede generar una serie de problemas: mayor estrés para las familias que regresan a casa después de un largo día de trabajo, preocupaciones por la seguridad al tener que caminar largas distancias durante la noche y dificultades adicionales para nuestros residentes mayores y las familias con niños pequeños. Nuestra propuesta no se trata simplemente de comodidad; es una petición para mejorar la calidad de vida, la seguridad y la continuidad de nuestra comunidad.

El impacto positivo de esta propuesta puede respaldarse con ejemplos de iniciativas similares implementadas en vecindarios como South Boston, donde el estacionamiento exclusivo para residentes ha contribuido a mejorar las condiciones y aumentar la satisfacción de la comunidad. Estas políticas han ayudado a preservar la integridad de los vecindarios y a reducir el tráfico innecesario, lo que beneficia a todos.

Nuestra comunidad ha demostrado resiliencia y capacidad de adaptación frente a muchos desafíos, pero el estacionamiento sigue siendo un problema constante que requiere soluciones y políticas bien pensadas. Al considerar nuestra solicitud de establecer horarios de estacionamiento exclusivo para residentes, la Ciudad de Boston puede demostrar su compromiso con el bienestar de la comunidad y con una ciudad más habitable.

Creemos que, mediante ajustes equilibrados en las políticas, incluyendo señalización adecuada y una aplicación estricta de las normas durante las horas de estacionamiento exclusivo para residentes, esta iniciativa puede implementarse con éxito sin causar interrupciones significativas a otros servicios de la ciudad ni a las áreas vecinas.

Su apoyo es fundamental para hacer de Jeffries Point un lugar más habitable para sus familias y sus residentes de toda la vida. Por favor, únase a nosotros firmando esta petición para lograr un cambio significativo y positivo en nuestro vecindario.

make-boston-s-3-a-m-last-call-permanent-.title: Make Boston's 3 A​.​M. last call permanent
make-boston-s-3-a-m-last-call-permanent-.description_full:
Boston has all the ingredients to be one of the best nightlife cities in the country.

We have world-class restaurants. Incredible cocktail bars. Amazing hotels. Historic neighborhoods. Some of the best universities in the world. Championship sports teams. A thriving music scene. And venues like Caveau, Mariel, Big Night Live, Royale, Memoire, The Grand, Roadrunner, MGM Music Hall at Fenway, House of Blues, Citizens House of Blues, and countless independent restaurants and bars that consistently bring energy, creativity, and talent to the city.

Boston regularly attracts internationally renowned DJs, musicians, chefs, and entertainers. People want to come here. People want to stay out. Businesses want to invest.

But every weekend, just as the city reaches its peak, everything is forced to wind down.

The recent 3 a.m. pilot showed what many of us already knew: there is demand for a later last call. Restaurants, bars, hospitality workers, artists, and patrons all benefit when people have the option to enjoy the city a little longer.

This isn't about forcing every business to stay open until 3 a.m. It's about giving businesses the choice to decide what makes sense for their customers.

A permanent 3 a.m. last call would:

  • Support hundreds of local restaurants, bars, venues, and small businesses.
  • Help Boston compete with cities like New York, Miami, Chicago, Nashville, Montreal, and London.
  • Attract more world-class artists, DJs, chefs, and entertainment who often prioritize cities with stronger nightlife.
  • Create more jobs and increase tax revenue.
  • Encourage visitors to stay in Boston instead of traveling elsewhere for nightlife.
  • Spread people out over a longer period, reducing the massive 2 a.m. rush for rideshares, taxis, and public transportation. 

Boston's nightlife isn't just about going out - it's about culture, hospitality, music, food, tourism, and thousands of people whose livelihoods depend on it. From neighborhood restaurants to iconic venues like Caveau and Mariel, these businesses help define the city's identity and deserve the flexibility to grow.

Boston is no longer just a college town. It is a global city with a world-class hospitality industry, and its policies should reflect that.

Let's give Boston the opportunity to reach its full potential.

Sign this petition to support a permanent 3 a.m. last call and help build a stronger, more vibrant, and more competitive Boston

We ask that you keep Coach and Pool Manager, Louis Barnes, at the Flaherty Pool.

This change is not only deeply unfair to a dedicated and successful employee, but it’s also an unfathomable cruelty to the kids who have been working hard this season in the pool and who are excited and committed to attending the Metro Championships at Boston University in March. We ask that BCYF allow Coach Louis to remain as the Flaherty Pool Manager and with the Flaherty Dolphins, preserving stability, opportunity, and growth for all the swimmers who depend on him and in the community he has helped create over the past 20 years.

We, the residents, business owners, property owners, and community leaders of Boston’s South End, strongly oppose the proposed conversion of the Foodie’s Market storefront into a private school, The Croft School. While we recognize that we cannot control whether Foodie’s remains in operation, we can and must oppose the continued loss of essential retail and food-use space in our neighborhood.

At minimum, this ground-floor storefront must remain dedicated to retail or food use. Foodie’s has long served as a walkable, community-serving grocery option, especially for neighbors who rely on nearby access to fresh food and daily necessities, including residents of Villa Victoria and the Cathedral Public Housing Development. The South End cannot afford to lose its only grocery-capable space to yet another school expansion, particularly as The Croft School already occupies four former retail spaces in the neighborhood (Stella Restaurant, Stella Café, Barre 3 South End, and Petco).

We call on the City of Boston, the Boston Planning & Development Agency (BPDA), the Zoning Board of Appeal, and the property owner to:

  1. Reject any proposed change of use that would convert the space from retail/food use into a private school or other institutional use
  2. Require that the space remain dedicated to retail or food use, prioritizing a grocery store or other neighborhood-serving food retailer, in keeping with the purpose of ground-floor commercial space
  3. Ensure a transparent public process, including community notification and meaningful neighborhood input before any approvals are granted
  4. Preserve an active, safe streetscape, including clear, lit storefront windows and a use that supports foot traffic, walkability, and public safety

improve-cyclist-safety-in-north-texas-co.title: Improve cyclist safety in North Texas communities
improve-cyclist-safety-in-north-texas-co.description_full:
We are a group of concerned cyclists, families, and residents from across North Texas. We are parents, children, professionals, students, business owners, veterans, and community members who ride and travel throughout Allen, Plano, Frisco, McKinney, Prosper, Celina, Little Elm, Richardson, Dallas, and surrounding communities. United by a common goal, we are advocating for safer roads for everyone.

Cycling has become an important part of life in North Texas. Every week, thousands of cyclists use our roads for recreation, fitness, transportation, charity events, and community activities. Unfortunately, our roads have become increasingly dangerous due to distracted driving, speeding, limited bicycle infrastructure, and a lack of awareness regarding cyclist safety.

Too many cyclists have been seriously injured or killed while riding legally on public roads. Every tragedy leaves families devastated and communities searching for answers. We believe these incidents are preventable and that meaningful action must be taken now.

We respectfully request that local governments, transportation departments, and law enforcement agencies work together to implement the following safety improvements:

• Expand dedicated and protected bicycle lanes throughout North Texas.

• Install highly visible “Share the Road” signs on major cycling routes.

• Add flashing and solar-powered cyclist warning signs in high-risk areas and popular cycling corridors.

• Improve intersection safety through enhanced pavement markings, cyclist crossing indicators, and better visibility.

• Increase enforcement of distracted driving, texting while driving, and other dangerous traffic violations.

• Develop public awareness campaigns educating motorists about safely sharing the road with cyclists.

• Create a regional task force involving city officials, transportation experts, law enforcement, and local cycling organizations.

• Conduct safety studies on roads with a history of cyclist crashes, injuries, and fatalities.

• Prioritize cyclist safety in future roadway planning and infrastructure projects.

This petition is not about cyclists versus drivers. It is about saving lives. Every cyclist is someone’s child, spouse, parent, friend, neighbor, or coworker. Everyone deserves to return home safely.

Our goal is simple: reduce injuries, prevent fatalities, and create safer roads for all who live, work, and travel throughout North Texas.

We respectfully ask our elected officials and community leaders to take immediate action before another preventable tragedy occurs.

Together, we can build a safer future for cyclists, motorists, pedestrians, and families across North Texas.

Please sign this petition and help us make our voices heard.

allen-city-council-city-manager-unfair-w.title: Unfair Water Billing Practices In The City Of Allen, TX
allen-city-council-city-manager-unfair-w.description_full:
For years there is consistently a large number of Allen residents that receive large water bills in September and October. We are very often met with the city explaining that we may have leaks or increased irrigation because of the heat. While we do agree irrigation can increase consumption some, there are too many instances of improbable and impossible consumption readings. Additionally, if we look back at months leading up to the high billed month they were billed less than they should have been. If we would be billed correctly that water would fall between $4.00-$6.26 per unit, but because it is being billed in one month with our tiered billing that same water is being billed as high as $14.10 a unit, resulting in bills hundreds or a thousand more than it should be. When we approach the city about this we are told that the meter doesn't lie. We are billed what the meter reads. The problem with this argument is that when meter readers either walk by or ride by in their cars and collect the TouchRead data it is sent to one computer that only one man is supposed to have access to. At that time he is able to see if the device collected the information, as well as a time stamp, a code that would say if it had to be manually entered or if it was electronically collected, and the reader ID of who read your meter. The computer will only store the current months data and what was billed the previous month. The previous billed is subtracted from the current read and that consumption is sent to billing. Once a 3rd month is collected the 2 months prior read is deleted. The only data we are left with is data sent to billing. We lose any ability to see if that data was edited or manually entered rather than read. We are told this is not important because they trust all of their employees and the data is not needed for billing so there is no reason to keep this information. This was the exact argument of the City of Austin before they had an audit that found some of their readers had obtained the supervisor's log in info and they were manually entering data on the computer rather than actual collections for months at a time. The city of Allen looks great on paper. With the finances we have we should not have such antiquated collections and record keepings. We currently have 7 readers who collect over 31,000 readings either by foot (or in their trucks, although that is against protocol). Riding in their trucks to collect is a violation of their rules. If one corner is being cut how can they so strongly say no others are. In 2011 the City did admit to WFAA that one reader was making up reads rather than reading true data. The city denied this on multiple occasions until one citizen finally caught the attention of the news. They settled with some of the complaints at that time. Coincidently, it was the same months we are claiming is still happening. We just want transparency. If there is nothing wrong on the city's side they should have no problem being open to these changes.

The goal: Independent Audit that would include billing periods May-November (*Edited from original request of October at the request of residents)

The goal: Multiple people verifying the computer that houses the collected data is being collected properly and no averages or estimates are being entered.

The goal: Storage of ALL data ever collected for a period of 3 years, including codes that would indicate if the data had been edited at any time or manually entered, regardless of its relevance to billing. 

We are not asking for anything but transparency. There is a very obvious problem with the city and it's time for them to step up and work to fix it. As citizens we deserve better than we are being treated by our city.  

 

I am updating this petition on 9/17/2020 with this information:

I became aware that they have GPS on the vehicles the readers use. There were many instances no one in our neighborhood saw a reader the entire month. But, on months he was seen he was always in his car reading from the window with the stick out of his driver’s side. So, I requested the GPS records for the days they claimed my meter was read. I requested May-October. May shows he collected on the 22nd, but my bill says it was the 23rd, June the bill reflects the same day it shows collected. July shows collected the 23rd, but the bill shows 24th. They were not able to find GPS records for August or September. September was the month my bill read 100,300 gallons. August was 51,800. This is when I began speaking out and have seen my bills become within expected range since. If they are claiming no information is ever changed once it’s loaded directly from the reading device, my dates should NEVER be different than the dates the device collected it. The fact that this still isn’t causing any movement at the city level is astonishing. I’ve had a lot of people ask me about the new billing system. THIS NEW SYSTEM DOENS’T FIX ANYTHING. The collection process is still the exact same. The process in which it’s reported to the billing department uses the same process. I was told they were going to try to include the time stamp with the exact date read on the bills. This would allow people the opportunity to know exactly when they came by, and that could be compared to cameras if there was debate. This did not happen.
